metadata.title: Claude, Demand Draft.
metadata.subtitle: The Demand-Draft Skill
metadata.purpose: Take apart the demand-draft Skill: not just what it does, but the design choice underneath — the model doesn't decide when a letter is safe, the checklist does. Lands the carry-out that predictable execution beats clever reasoning when the stakes are legal.

beats.narration_text: Someone asked me to take this apart. When Claude drafts a demand letter, is it just running a language model over the facts? Or does a check have to clear first? Because those are two completely different products.

TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('write' -> 'check first', landing 'does it just write?' -> 'does it just check first?') lands on screen. NOTE: triggerWords must be a SINGLE whitespace-delimited token — the component matches per-token, not phrase-wise; an earlier 'just write' (two words) never matched and the correction silently never fired.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A Skill is a folder Claude reads before it acts. This one is called demand-draft. Its one file, SKILL.md, holds the whole instruction set in plain English — no compiled binaries, no hidden config. Claude reads the file, then executes. The file is the program. They optimized for reviewability at the expense of concealment: any lawyer can open the folder and see exactly what Claude will do.

The instructions live in a Steps section. Claude reads each step in order and runs it — read the file, execute each step, return the result. Linear by default. No branching, unless a step explicitly says so. That's the design choice: predictable execution over clever reasoning. You know what it's going to do before it does it.

production_viz.label: READ, EXECUTE, RETURN
production_viz.caption: linear — no branching unless a step says so

beats.narration_text: One instruction in there is not up for interpretation. Before any letter gets drafted, four checks have to clear — privilege, Rule 408, waiver, and admission. Only after all four clear does Claude produce the draft, as a docx file, with a post-send checklist and an offer to open a matter. This works if you value predictable safety over model judgment. It fails if you want Claude to freelance.

Here's the take. Claude isn't the one deciding when a demand letter is ready to send. The checklist is — privilege, Rule 408, waiver, admission — and all four have to clear first. That's not a limitation. That's the point.

props.quote: Claude isn't deciding when a demand letter is ready to send — the checklist is: privilege, Rule 408, waiver, and admission all have to clear first.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini right now. I have a completed intake for a demand letter — read the demand-draft skill, and before you draft anything, walk me through the four checks you'll run first: privilege, Rule 408, waiver, admission. For each one, tell me what facts from my intake you'd need to clear it, and what you'd do if the intake didn't have them. Go deeper: ask the model to redesign the same checklist for a cease-and-desist letter instead — what changes, what stays, and why.

For each check, tell me what specific facts you'd need from my intake to clear it, and what you'd do if the intake didn't have them.
